Poisson autoregressive (PAR) models serve as valuable tools for analyzing count time series data exhibiting strong temporal dependence. This paper introduces a time-varying extension of the PAR(p) framework, termed the TVPAR(p) model. We define the model and its associated filtering and smoothing algorithms, and we develop an efficient estimation approach combining an Expectation-Maximization algorithm with Bayesian inference. The proposed method allows for the flexible, data-driven recovery of time-varying autoregressive parameters and their underlying distributions. We evaluate the performance of our approach through a Monte Carlo simulation study and apply the model to real-world datasets to investigate the dynamic nature of dependence structures in count data.

This paper presents a novel approach to measuring aerosol optical depth (AOD) using stellar photometry, a technique originally designed for atmospheric correction in ground-based optical spectroscopy. Unlike traditional methods that rely on extensive calibration against space-borne reference data, our approach requires no such calibration. Instead, it leverages the well-established variability of stellar colors caused by interstellar dust along the line of sight. By utilizing a simple color-magnitude relationship, we can retrieve AOD values directly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this uncalibrated method through observations of the Pleiades cluster, showing that it achieves accuracy comparable to those methods dependent on satellite calibration.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are a key computational tool for exploring the conformational space of biomolecules. However, standard MD methods often struggle with efficiency when sampling configurations for large biomolecules, such as proteins. This study introduces a new integrator designed for overdamped Langevin dynamics, which combines high accuracy with exceptional efficiency. The proposed method achieves an order of accuracy that is optimal for the forces, while simultaneously delivering robust sampling of the Boltzmann distribution. We demonstrate the superior performance of this new integrator through extensive numerical experiments, including tests on harmonic oscillators, a double-well system, and conformational sampling of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease.

This paper examines the suitability of human reference data for assessing automatic image descriptions, noting that while widely used, these references are not flawless. We introduce a new dataset comprising 10,000 descriptions generated by a large language model for the Flickr30k, MSCOCO, and MS-COCO test sets, which were subsequently evaluated by human annotators. Our findings reveal that although human references are generally reliable, they occasionally contain errors, and relying on them exclusively can introduce biases into evaluation metrics. To address these issues, we propose a method for detecting and correcting such errors. Ultimately, we advocate for the development of more robust evaluation protocols that mitigate the limitations inherent in current human reference data.

Defining quantum field theory complexity remains a significant challenge, particularly for Conformal Field Theories (CFTs). We introduce a novel approach to define the complexity of CFTs by utilizing the Euler-Arnold equations. These equations govern the time evolution of the simplectic form within the space of CFTs, which are treated as a Finsler manifold. By applying this framework to the $\phi^4$ theory in $d=3$, we demonstrate that the associated Euler-Arnold equations are integrable.

We examine the consequences of the Baryon Number Violating (BNV) Baryomagnetic Monopole (BMM) interaction, which is anticipated to be operative at the TeV scale. This interaction is hypothesized to be responsible for the BNV decay of the BMM, a phenomenon that may be observable in upcoming high-energy collider experiments. We demonstrate that the BMM interaction induces BNV decays for various heavy baryons and mesons containing top quarks, charm quarks, and bottom quarks. These predicted decay modes are expected to be detectable at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

This study extends the wideband waveforming technique for simultaneous data and energy transfer, originally proposed for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems, to cover SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations. The extended approach leverages both multipath diversity and multiple antennas to enhance energy-harvesting efficiency and data-transmission rates. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed wideband waveforming scheme consistently outperforms conventional orthogonal methods across various scenarios. Specifically, the scheme achieves a 100% increase in energy-harvesting efficiency and a 20% improvement in data-transmission rates when utilizing a 20 MHz bandwidth with a single transmit antenna.

Achieving a fit of parton distribution functions (PDFs) requires the integration of experimental data with theoretical predictions for PDF-dependent physical processes. Currently, the theoretical framework for these predictions is provided by the xFitter project, which utilizes the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO framework. This paper outlines a new, automated pipeline designed to generate theoretical predictions for PDF fits, specifically targeting LHC data. The approach relies on the use of matrix elements at leading order (LO) or next-to-leading order (NLO) within the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO framework, with parton showers and hadronization effects neglected. The pipeline operates by querying a database of LO and NLO cross-sections for relevant LHC processes, filtering for those applicable to the specific fit, and subsequently generating the corresponding analysis code. This code is then adapted to align with the format required by the EPSOS fitting program. We demonstrate the application of this pipeline by reproducing the analysis code for the MSW2017 PDF fit.

This study examines the linearized response of a turbulent jet flame to acoustic forcing within a confined domain, utilizing a model grounded in an active flame framework. The approach incorporates a nonlinear closure for the reaction rate, which is linearized to facilitate the analysis. Results indicate that the flame's response to acoustic forcing is predominantly driven by the interaction between the vorticity and entropy waves generated by the inlet disturbances. These disturbances are amplified as they traverse the domain, subsequently triggering Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities at the shear layer. The linearized reaction rate closure is shown to be capable of capturing the resulting flame dynamics, with the response being significantly modulated by the inlet conditions.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) emerges as a nonlocal extension of general relativity, incorporating nonlocal effects into the constitutive relations that connect the energy-momentum tensor to the metric. In this framework, matter is treated as an external source, and the theory is defined by a nonlocal constitutive relation. This paper demonstrates that NLG can be reformulated as a local theory by introducing fundamental tetrads, which serve as the nonlocal counterparts to the standard tetrads found in special and general relativity. By expressing the nonlocal constitutive relation through these fundamental tetrads, the theory becomes local, albeit with an increased number of gravitational degrees of freedom. The resulting local formulation is mathematically equivalent to the nonlocal theory and is expressed as a local theory of nonmetric gravity.

The LHC has provided a unique opportunity to study small systems, such as proton-lead (pPb) and lead-lead (PbPb) collisions, at unprecedented center-of-mass energies. This paper offers a concise overview of the experimental results obtained from these small system collisions at the LHC. The discussion covers the measurement of particle production, collective flow phenomena, and jet quenching effects. Additionally, the text explores the theoretical interpretations of these findings, with a specific focus on the role of initial-state gluon saturation.

Neutron star X-ray binaries in the Milky Way are categorized into two groups: those that exhibit recurring outbursts, known as transients, and those that remain dim and steady, referred to as quiescent sources. This paper examines the connection between the recurrence intervals of transient outbursts and the physical characteristics of the Galactic Centre's quiescent neutron star systems. We develop a statistical framework to forecast the likelihood of previously detected transients reappearing within a specific timeframe, utilizing a sample of 24 well-documented Galactic transient events. Our findings indicate that the probability of a specific transient recurring within a given period declines as the observation window extends. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the duration of an X-ray outburst serves as a reliable predictor for a system's future recurrence behavior. Consequently, we propose that the nature of the Galactic Centre's quiescent neutron star binaries can be deduced by analyzing their X-ray luminosity alongside the total time these systems have been monitored.

Bipartite vertex splitting involves transforming a given bipartite graph $G$ into a new bipartite graph $H$ by duplicating vertices from one of $G$'s independent sets. These copies are then reconnected to form a new graph $H$, which must contain an independent set of the same cardinality as the original graph $G$. This paper investigates the problem of minimizing the number of required duplications to achieve such a transformation. The authors establish that this problem is NP-hard and demonstrate its W[1]-hardness with respect to the solution size. Furthermore, they prove the problem admits a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm when parameterized by the number of duplications. Specifically, the algorithm runs in $O^*(2^k)$ time, where $k$ represents the number of duplications.

This paper introduces HyperDegrade, a novel technique designed to reduce the effective CPU frequency of an adversary's core by a factor of 100 without causing a system crash. By leveraging thermal throttling and performance degradation, HyperDegrade enables a single core to be slowed down significantly while other cores continue to operate at full speed. We evaluated this approach across various Intel architectures, achieving effective frequency reductions ranging from 10x to 100x. Specifically, we demonstrated that a 3.2 GHz core could be throttled to an effective 32 MHz. The resulting performance drop was so severe that the affected core could no longer execute the HyperDegrade process itself. We believe this capability offers a practical solution for mitigating remote code execution attacks, as it allows a victim system to neutralize an adversary's computational advantage by slowing their core to the point where executing malicious payloads becomes infeasible.

We introduce a novel unknotting operation applicable to both classical and welded links. This operation involves removing a crossing and reconnecting the strands via a specific over/under configuration. We demonstrate that the operation is non-invertive and establish an upper bound for the Kauffman polynomial after its application. Additionally, we provide a complete characterization of the operation for classical links and illustrate its utility in proving the non-isotopy of certain welded links.

We examine the strategic coordination of multiple tasks among robots operating on a regular network, where agents face trade-offs between their own task execution and collective task performance. The objective is to maximize the sum of individual and collective utilities, with the latter representing a shared reward for all agents. We establish that the resulting strategic coordination problem is a generalized potential game, which guarantees the existence of pure strategy Nash equilibria. Furthermore, we characterize the conditions under which these equilibria are Pareto optimal and provide a closed-form solution for the optimal coordination strategy. Our analysis reveals that the optimal approach involves a specific threshold policy, contingent upon the network's topology, the agents' utility functions, and the underlying task dynamics.

This paper presents a novel proof of the Higman-Neumann-Neumann (HNNN) theorem, which establishes that if a group $G$ embeds into the wreath product $H \wr K$, then $G$ also embeds into the restricted direct product $H^K \times K$. The authors demonstrate that this result serves as a special case of a broader theorem regarding HNN extensions. Their approach relies on a specific HNN extension of the target group $H^K \times K$, utilizing the fact that the HNNN theorem itself can be derived from HNN extension theory. The proof is constructed by combining the HNN version of the HNNN theorem with the HNN version of Higman's embedding theorem.

Sloshing-Sagnac interferometers represent a novel variation of Sagnac configurations, designed to boost the high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors. In this design, a sloshing mode emerges from the interaction between counter-propagating light beams and the rotating test mass within the Sagnac loop. This paper examines the sloshing-Sagnc configuration, analyzing how the sloshing mode influences high-frequency sensitivity and exploring the potential for enhancing it. Our findings indicate that the sloshing mode significantly improves sensitivity at high frequencies, with the degree of enhancement contingent upon the rotation speed of the test mass. We project that incorporating a 10 kg test mass rotating at 1 rad/s into the second generation of High-LIGO detectors could elevate high-frequency sensitivity by a factor of 2.5.

Extra-large MIMO (XL-MIMO) systems are poised to be a key enabler for sixth-generation wireless networks, offering unprecedented data rates and energy efficiency. However, the vast physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays introduce significant challenges regarding protocol design, particularly for random access (RA), which is critical for initial system connectivity. This paper investigates the non-overlapping visibility regions that emerge in XL-MIMO scenarios, a phenomenon absent in conventional compact arrays. We develop a comprehensive framework to model the XL-MIMO random access protocol, explicitly incorporating these visibility constraints. Our analysis reveals that these non-overlapping regions substantially influence system performance, notably degrading throughput and increasing access delays. To counteract these effects, we propose an optimized protocol design that leverages the unique visibility characteristics to enhance overall system efficiency.

Although neural language models have largely superseded $N$-grams, this study finds that $N$-grams remain effective for specific tasks like TREC factoid question answering. We introduce a residual neural architecture designed to learn the deviations from an $N$-gram baseline, enabling the combination of neural capabilities with the efficiency of $N$-grams. Experiments on the TREC chatbot dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms standard neural approaches while reducing training time by 40% and achieving a 1% gain in exact match scores compared to a strong baseline neural model. Additionally, we present a hierarchical residual extension for $N$-grams, which further enhances performance.

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology has been proposed as a method to enhance the accuracy of vote tallies for electronic voting systems. This paper offers a critical evaluation of that proposal, arguing that the claim of improved accuracy is unsupported. The authors introduce iOCR, an informed OCR framework designed to mitigate errors caused by the distinctive visual characteristics of ballots. Empirical results indicate that iOCR substantially outperforms standard OCR methods, reducing error rates by 20% to 40% across various tested ballots. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the specific ballot features responsible for recognition failures are not unique to electronic voting systems but are also present in paper ballots processed manually by human election workers. Consequently, the paper concludes that the original assertion—that electronic ballots require special OCR handling to achieve greater accuracy than manual counts—is unfounded.

Global atmospheric circulation is governed by the interplay between the Coriolis force, buoyancy, and the Rossby number, which itself depends on the ratio of inertial to Coriolis forces. This study employs simplified global circulation models (SGCMs) to examine how circulation regimes shift as surface friction and planetary rotation rates vary. We find that in the absence of friction, the circulation is cyclostrophic and characterized by super-rotation in the equatorial region. Conversely, increasing surface friction or reducing the rotation rate promotes turbulence and geostrophic balance, with the latter dominating at high latitudes. We analyze the structural differences between these geostrophic and cyclostrophic regimes, focusing on the transition from geostrophic turbulence to equatorial super-rotation. Our results indicate that friction acts as a primary driver for this transition, with the onset of equatorial super-rotation occurring at a critical friction threshold.

This paper presents regularized integral representations for the reciprocal Gamma function, which are derived from Cauchy's integral formula by applying a regularization technique to the logarithm of the Gamma function. These new representations are shown to be equivalent to those originally established by Ramanujan. Furthermore, the derived formulas are utilized to generate a series of novel integral representations for the logarithm of the Gamma function and its derivatives.

Hydrodynamic theories provide a valuable framework for describing the macroscopic behavior of quantum fluids, yet standard approaches often encounter difficulties when applied to systems with strong interactions. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a novel hydrodynamic formalism for interacting Bose gases based on phase-space Wigner quantum hydrodynamics. This approach incorporates quantum corrections expressed as a systematic expansion in powers of $\hbar$. We derive the governing hydrodynamic equations up to fourth order in $\hbar$, which includes a viscosity tensor and a heat conductivity tensor that are non-local in time. These non-local transport coefficients are explicitly defined through the Wigner function and the quantum-corrected density matrix. We demonstrate that our derived equations are capable of accurately predicting the dynamics of a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) during a free expansion, as well as the shock wave formation resulting from supersonic flow.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across numerous domains, yet their extensive parameter counts often lead to high computational costs and substantial memory usage. Knowledge Distillation (KD) offers a promising solution by enabling compact student models to learn from large teacher models, thereby reducing complexity while preserving performance. Although the core objective of KD is to distill output logits, recent research indicates that incorporating intermediate representations—such as hidden layers and attention mechanisms—can further enhance the efficiency and accuracy of student models. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of intermediate representation learning within KD frameworks. We categorize existing methods based on the types of representations distilled, analyze their respective loss functions, and examine the architectural designs of both teacher and student models. Furthermore, we explore the integration of knowledge learning with other tasks, including multi-task learning, domain adaptation, and few-shot learning. Finally, we identify key challenges and propose potential future research directions in this evolving field.

This paper introduces a compact function representation designed to accelerate the computation of graphical models, specifically targeting the challenges of constrained optimization and exact Maximum Posterior Estimation (MPE). We demonstrate that our method achieves a significant reduction in space complexity compared to standard approaches. Furthermore, we show that this efficiency translates into practical performance gains: constrained optimization tasks are solved approximately 1.5 times faster, and the exact algorithm for constrained MPE achieves a 10-fold speedup over the most efficient existing exact method.

We establish a connection between the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and the Racah algebra $u_n$ by demonstrating that $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is isomorphic to the quotient $u_n / (u_n f_1)$, where $f_1$ denotes the first Casimir operator of the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Building upon this isomorphism, we derive a closed-form expression for the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$.

Statistical significance testing is a vital tool for evaluating the reliability of results in data analysis, particularly in high-dimensional contexts like genomics and natural language processing. While numerous methods exist for significance tests on unstructured data, the specialized nature of structured data—such as gene regulatory networks or semantic similarity matrices—requires tailored approaches. This paper introduces an efficient algorithm designed to compute the precise p-value for significance tests applied to statistics with specific structures, including linear combinations, monotonic transformations, and rank-based metrics. The algorithm achieves this by decomposing the statistic into constituent parts, evaluating significance for each individually, and synthesizing the results. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the method is both highly accurate and efficient, with a median runtime of 0.01 seconds across 10,000 permutations for various structured statistics.

We report a study of the triangular flow, $v_3$, in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV using a (3+1)-dimensional multiphase transport (AMPT) model. In this investigation, $v_3$ is extracted from the azimuthal distribution of charged-particle yields, which are generated via a Monte Carlo simulation of the AMPT framework. Our findings indicate that $v_3$ exhibits a linear correlation with initial geometric anisotropies, $\langle \epsilon_3 \rangle$, averaged over multiplicity. Additionally, we observe that the ratio $v_3 / v_2$ increases with the initial eccentricity $\langle \epsilon_3 \rangle$. These results are compared against predictions from ideal and viscous hydrodynamic models.

Soccer represents a strategic game of high complexity, where the vast state and action spaces, combined with the difficulty of defining reward functions, have historically hindered the application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL). This study introduces a novel approach to optimize soccer strategies by employing a hierarchical DRL architecture. The proposed method utilizes a deep neural network to map game states to action values, which are subsequently processed by a hierarchical policy network to generate optimal decisions. To evaluate the model, the authors reconstructed the reward function based on real-world soccer data, simulating various scenarios to test the system's ability to learn from different incentives. Results indicate that the hierarchical architecture successfully adapts to distinct reward configurations, with the model trained to favor attacking plays demonstrating a marked increase in offensive actions compared to baseline strategies. Furthermore, the learned policies exhibit a significant reduction in suboptimal decisions during critical game moments, such as penalty kicks and final minutes, thereby enhancing overall strategic efficiency.

This study presents the remote operation of a single-point Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV) system designed for acquiring two-dimensional (2D) surface velocity data. By integrating a scanning mechanism with an automated stage, the setup enables the collection of 2D velocity maps from a target area. The resulting data is processed to generate full-field displacement, strain, and mode shape visualizations. The system was validated by remotely measuring the dynamic response of a cantilever beam under harmonic excitation. Results demonstrated that the automated 2D LDV system successfully captured mode shapes and provided accurate displacement, strain, and mode shape information.

We establish the spectral and orbital stability for ground state solutions to a Klein--Gordon equation with an anharmonic nonlinearity in one spatial dimension. Our analysis reveals that the associated linearized operator possesses a finite number of negative eigenvalues and exhibits a simple positive eigenvalue exceeding the mass threshold. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the linearized dynamics are well-behaved at infinity, allowing for a complete characterization of the spectrum.

At the Belle II experiment, we examine the potential for observing the decay of $B$ mesons into a $K^0_S$ meson and an undetectable particle, represented as $B \to K^0_S + X$. This process serves as a signature for producing neutral particles that escape detection, such as neutrinos or dark sector candidates like dark photons or axion-like particles (ALPs). We present a search for this specific decay mode using a dataset collected at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $194\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. By analyzing events with a $K^0_S \to \pi^+ \pi^-$ candidate, we establish upper limits on the branching fraction for $B^0 \to K^0 X$ at the $90\%$ confidence level. These constraints apply across various hypotheses regarding the invisible particle's mass and its interaction properties. Specifically, if the invisible particle is a dark photon ($A'$), the search constrains the $B^0 \to K^0 A'$ production cross-section multiplied by the decay probability $\mathcal{P}(A' \to \text{invisible})$ to be below $1.2 \times 10^{-6}$ for masses between $0.01$ and $1.0\,\mathrm{GeV}/c^2$. Contextualized language models (CLMs) have recently been proposed as a promising approach for identifying semantic shifts in historical texts. This study offers a comprehensive evaluation of CLMs for this purpose, contrasting their performance against non-contextualized baselines such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText. Our analysis reveals that CLMs do not consistently outperform these traditional methods. Specifically, BERT and RoBERTa frequently fail to surpass GloVe, while XLNet and ERNIE often underperform relative to Word2Vec. We attribute these results to the fact that CLMs are optimized for contextual prediction tasks, which may not align with semantic change detection objectives. Consequently, we advocate for the development of specialized contextualized architectures explicitly designed for this detection task.

We examine the mass and spin characteristics of possible ultralight bosons, which may arise from the spontaneous symmetry breaking of an additional $U(1)$ gauge symmetry, by analyzing the masses and spins of heavy quasar black holes. Our analysis indicates that a wide range of masses and spins for both black holes and the hypothetical bosons can be simultaneously accounted for through a single, unified framework. Specifically, we demonstrate that the superradiant instability mechanism effectively explains the observed properties of black holes across masses exceeding $10^8 M_{\odot}$ when considering axion-like bosons with masses greater than $10^{-13}$ eV.

We present a numerical study of a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to a constant force and linear damping, utilizing imaginary time path integrals combined with a Metropolis Monte Carlo algorithm. By applying a simple discretization scheme in imaginary time, the resulting simulation becomes a high-dimensional classical statistical mechanics problem. Our numerical results demonstrate that the Euclidean time correlation function for the damped, driven system exhibits exponential decay in its long-time limit, a behavior consistent with the known analytical solution.

This paper introduces a novel relational quantum logic designed to verify quantum programs, termed Quantum Relational Hoare Logic with Expectations (QRHLE). Distinct from traditional quantum logics that rely on predicates, QRHLE utilizes expectations—functions mapping postconditions to probabilities—enabling the verification of probabilistic properties such as success rates and average values. The logic adheres to a relational framework, allowing for the simultaneous verification of multiple quantum programs to establish equivalence and other relational invariants. We formally define QRHLE, prove its soundness, and demonstrate its utility by verifying key quantum algorithms, including Grover's search and Shor's factoring.

Vector magnetograms are crucial for understanding solar physics and forecasting space weather, yet the remote sensing techniques used to derive vector magnetic fields from spectropolarimetric observations introduce subtle errors. These errors stem from the inversion of the radiative transfer equation, which relies on assumptions regarding atmospheric models and the completeness of the input data. Consequently, the inversion process can generate spurious magnetic signals, known as biases, particularly in the presence of noise or when atmospheric models are imperfect. This study employs a novel methodology to detect and reduce these biases by utilizing a dataset of 1,000 synthetic images generated from a 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulation. The approach involves reconstructing the inversion process to recover the simulated magnetic fields and comparing the results against the known ground truth. The analysis reveals that noise and atmospheric modeling inaccuracies both contribute significantly to the emergence of these biases. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that applying regularization techniques during the inversion effectively mitigates the issue, resulting in a reduction of the average bias by approximately 50%.

This paper investigates the concept of timelike Bertrand curves within $\mathbb{R}^3_1$. We first establish a fundamental theorem regarding these curves, demonstrating that a timelike Bertrand curve is characterized as a curve of constant curvature. Subsequently, we explore the relationship between these curves and helices, deriving a specific formula for the Frenet-Serret apparatus associated with a timelike Bertrand curve. Finally, we provide a concrete example illustrating a timelike Bertrand curve defined in $\mathbb{R}^3_1$.

This study investigates how altering the loss function influences the performance of deep learning models designed for classification tasks. The research compares the cross-entropy loss against the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, examining their respective impacts on model outcomes. The authors explore the theoretical connections between these two losses and analyze how specific modifications to the target distribution affect the resulting models. Findings indicate that while the KL divergence often yields superior results when the target distribution is well-estimated, the cross-entropy loss remains more robust and effective when target estimates are uncertain or noisy.

Achieving commonsense reasoning in artificial intelligence remains a significant hurdle, particularly when navigating the complex "if-then" relationships that define everyday logic. This research introduces ATOMIC, an extensive commonsense reasoning dataset designed to capture these conditional machine commonsense relations. ATOMIC employs a knowledge graph framework to explicitly model the connections between triggers (the "if" conditions) and their corresponding responses (the "then" outcomes). The dataset encompasses four primary relation categories: ATOMIC-NA, ATOMIC-RE, ATOMIC-UN, and ATOMIC-AB, each representing distinct modes of logical entailment. To facilitate the learning of these relations, the authors developed ATOMIC-Net, a neural architecture capable of reasoning over the knowledge graph. Evaluation results demonstrate that training on ATOMIC substantially enhances a model's ability to identify new, unseen conditional commonsense relations, with the ATOMIC-AB category specifically proving effective for deriving novel logical connections.

Video prediction serves as a significant challenge in computer vision, aiming to forecast future frames from a video sequence. This paper introduces a new approach to video prediction that leverages a dual representation, combining an image-based component with an optical flow-based component. The method employs a recurrent neural network (RNN) to process this dual representation, enabling the model to learn both static and dynamic elements within the video. The proposed architecture is designed to be end-to-end trainable and does not require pre-trained models. Experiments conducted on two standard datasets—MSE and UCF-QSP—demonstrate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, qualitative results indicate that the proposed model generates more realistic video predictions compared to other methods.

Let $G$ be a connected graph with vertex set $V(G)$. For any subset $W \subseteq V(G)$, the metric dimension of $G$ relative to $W$, denoted by $\dim(G;W)$, is defined as the smallest cardinality of a subset $S \subseteq V(G)$ such that every pair of distinct vertices in $W$ can be distinguished by at least one vertex in $S$. This paper investigates the truncated metric dimension of finite graphs, which is the function mapping each subset $W$ to the value $\min\{\dim(G;W), |W|-1\}$. We establish a formula for the truncated metric dimension of finite trees and provide a complete characterization for finite cycles. Additionally, we determine the exact values for paths, complete graphs, complete bipartite graphs, and other specific graph types. Finally, we examine the monotonicity of the truncated metric dimension and explore its relationship with the standard metric dimension.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a primary method for diagnosing cardiac disorders, yet the automatic classification of heart sounds remains challenging due to additive noise and cardiac-specific distortions. This study introduces a novel Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture designed to simultaneously mitigate both additive noise and cardiac morphological distortions. The proposed model employs parallel convolutional layers to extract features from the input spectrogram, which are subsequently merged and processed by a fully connected layer to generate the final prediction. Evaluated on the widely used MIT-Stamford dataset, the new architecture achieves a 99.3% F1-score, representing a 0.4% improvement over the prior state-of-the-art method.

We utilized a non-LTE radiative transfer model to examine the formation of carbon monoxide ($CO$) and atomic carbon ($C\,\text{i}$) spectral lines within the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies. Our analysis indicates that the $C\,\text{i}$ lines are predominantly generated in the subthermal regime, a condition where the upper levels of the $C\,\text{i}$ $^3P$-multiplet fail to reach thermal equilibrium with the local kinetic temperature. We demonstrate that the intensity ratio of the $C\,\text{i}$ $^3P_1 \rightarrow ^3P_0$ transition to the $CO$ $J=2 \rightarrow 1$ line serves as a robust diagnostic for estimating the kinetic temperature in galaxies containing significant molecular gas. This method offers a valuable alternative to traditional techniques, such as those relying on $C\,\text{i}$ $^3P_1 \rightarrow ^3P_0$ and $^3P_0 \rightarrow ^3P_0$ ratios, which are often hindered by uncertainties regarding the excitation of the $^3P_1$ state.

We introduce the ASEP speed process, a stochastic counterpart to the Hopf-Cole transformation for the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP). This dynamic object allows for the representation of solutions to the Kardar-Parisi-Schwing (KPZ) equation via the ASEP's solution to the associated Burgers equation. We establish the existence of the ASEP speed process and demonstrate its utility in deriving a novel representation for the solution to the KPZ equation. Furthermore, we prove that the ASEP speed process is almost surely constant over time when the initial data for the ASEP are drawn from a Bernoulli distribution.

Mathematical models serve as a vital instrument for analyzing and forecasting the progression of infectious disease epidemics. This paper offers a retrospective examination of the mathematical frameworks employed during the current SARS-CoV-2 outbreak, with a specific focus on compartmental models. We explore the theoretical foundations of these models, the methodologies used to estimate their parameters, and the strategies for fitting them to empirical data. Furthermore, we assess the practical applications of these models, including the estimation of key epidemiological indicators such as the basic reproductive number ($R_0$), the identification of optimal intervention measures, and the projection of future infection trajectories. Finally, we address the inherent constraints of these models and discuss how they can be effectively utilized to guide public health policy decisions.

The correlation between stellar mass ($M_*$)$ and specific star formation rate (sSFR)$ exhibits a negative trend across the local universe, which flattens at masses exceeding $10^{10} M_{\odot}$. While bulges are widely recognized as the primary structural component responsible for this turnover, the precise physical mechanism linking bulges to reduced star formation remains unclear. To investigate this, we utilized a sample of 1,000 local galaxies from the CALIFA survey to examine the relationship between bulge-to-total mass ratios ($B/T$)$ and sSFR$ at constant $M_*$$. Our findings reveal that sSFR$ declines as $B/T$ increases, confirming that bulges drive the flattening of the $M_*$$-sSFR$ relation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that bulges influence star formation rates through two distinct pathways: a global effect, where bulgy galaxies tend to be older and thus intrinsically less active, and a local effect, where bulges directly suppress star formation within their own disks.

This paper introduces a novel multitask learning framework designed for cross-lingual sentiment analysis. The proposed approach employs a shared hidden layer to capture universal linguistic characteristics across languages, complemented by task-specific output layers to handle distinct sentiment classification challenges. Additionally, the model incorporates a regularization term to mitigate overfitting. Experiments conducted on English and Chinese datasets demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing cross-lingual approaches, achieving a 3.4% increase in F1 score for English and a 4.1% improvement for Chinese.

The Sun's rotation rate has decreased significantly over the course of its main-sequence evolution, a phenomenon widely attributed to magnetic braking and internal angular momentum transport mechanisms. While the precise details of these mechanisms remain uncertain, the Sun's current slow spin is well established. Here, we report the discovery of a star, HD 179949, that exhibits a rapid rotation rate comparable to the Sun's zero-age main-sequence velocity yet displays chromospheric activity levels typical of much younger, rapidly rotating stars. This combination of high rotation and elevated activity indicates that HD 179949 has likely accreted a giant planet, an event which would have introduced additional mass and angular momentum to the stellar surface. We explore the implications of this finding for models of magnetic braking, internal angular momentum transport, and the history of planet formation.

The rapid proliferation of social media has significantly facilitated the dissemination of misinformation, creating a pressing need for automated detection systems. While existing research has largely concentrated on textual news, the rise of image-based content on platforms like Facebook and WeChat has introduced a critical gap: the lack of effective detection methods for image-driven misinformation. This study proposes a novel framework designed to identify emergent fake news generated through images. The approach employs a meta-learning architecture that integrates a multimodal neural process network, enabling the model to learn from unseen news events without requiring event-specific training data. By combining a meta-learner with a multimodal neural process network, the system effectively handles the detection of news from novel events. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate that this framework substantially outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 10.4% increase in F1 scores for binary classification and a 12.1% improvement for multi-label scenarios.

The invention of Golay complementary arrays (GCAs) extends the well-known Golay complementary sequences (GCSs), which have been extensively utilized in radar, sonar, wireless communications, and signal processing. This paper presents novel constructions of GCAs, including new generalized forms of GCAs derived from specific Golay complementary matrices (GCMs). Additionally, the authors introduce generalized GCAs constructed from a pair of Golay complementary matrices (GCMs) and a set of GCAs with uniform shifts. These proposed constructions yield significantly larger GCAs compared to existing methods. Finally, several high-dimensional GCAs are generated using the presented generalized constructions.

This study introduces a novel framework for synthetic brain lesion generation, termed PAVAE, which combines a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVAE). The proposed architecture integrates a conditional GAN (cGAN) within its decoder to enhance the realism of synthetic lesions. To specifically target lesion characteristics, the model employs a dedicated lesion discriminator that operates in conjunction with the primary image discriminator. The resulting synthetic T1, T2, and T1-weighted post-contrast (T1pc) MRI images are subsequently utilized to train deep learning models for downstream tasks, including lesion segmentation and classification. Experiments conducted on the ADNI dataset demonstrate that the synthetic images generated by PAVAE achieve superior realism compared to standard methods. Furthermore, models trained on these synthetic images exhibit enhanced performance in downstream applications, surpassing those trained using only real data. Notably, the synthetic images also facilitate the training of segmentation and classification models for rare lesions, such as those associated with aneurysms.

Feature extraction serves as a foundational technique in computer vision, yet existing methods often lack the flexibility to adapt to new tasks. This paper introduces a novel framework based on contrastive learning designed to address this shortcoming. The proposed method trains a neural network to learn representations for a source dataset using contrastive learning, which are subsequently utilized for classification on a target dataset without requiring retraining of the network's weights. The framework operates by first training a network on a source dataset to learn contrastive representations, followed by the training of a classifier on a target dataset using these learned representations. The resulting classifying model is then employed for final classification. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods across various datasets.

Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their training data is often riddled with noise and hallucinations, particularly regarding factual knowledge. While recent approaches attempt to mitigate these issues by incorporating structured knowledge graphs (KGs) during pre-training, they frequently fail to balance the retention of the model's original linguistic strengths with the acquisition of new factual information. To bridge this gap, we introduce **SKILL** (Structured Knowledge Infusion for Large Language Models), a method designed to inject structured knowledge into an already trained LLM. Unlike prior techniques that rely on extensive retraining, SKILL operates as a post-training approach, requiring only a single pass over the knowledge graph. Our framework employs a two-stage process: first, it constructs a specialized KG-aware vocabulary to align the LLM with the graph's entities and relations; second, it utilizes contrastive learning to refine the model's representations. Extensive experiments across diverse knowledge graphs and various downstream tasks demonstrate that SKILL consistently outperforms existing methods. Notably, SKILL-1B achieves a +1.2% improvement on average on knowledge graph completion tasks and a +1.5% gain on open-domain question answering compared to the current state-of-the-art.

We examine the non-linear charged non-rotating AdS black hole thermodynamics using the non-linear Born-Infeld electromagnetic action. Our analysis reveals that the non-linear charge significantly influences the shadow radius of a rotating AdS black hole, causing it to shrink as the charge increases. We find a strong correlation between the shadow radius and the non-linear charge, which allows for the potential measurement of this non-linear parameter via black hole shadow observations. Additionally, we explore the stability of these non-linear charged AdS black holes through quasinormal mode analysis and Hawking-Page phase transitions. Our results indicate that non-linear charge accelerates the onset of thermal instability and reduces the temperature required for the Hawking-Page transition.

We examine the evolution of quantum entanglement and the emergence of synchronization within the continuous-variable entangled state of a two-mode squeezed vacuum system, as observed through the Wigner function and various tomographic slices. Our analysis demonstrates that entanglement manifests itself through the non-separability of the Wigner function and specific tomographic cross-sections. Conversely, the onset of synchronization becomes evident via the appearance of distinct entanglement signatures within the Wigner function and other reconstructed slices.

This report presents the first observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode and provides evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ process. The analysis utilizes proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at $\sqrt{s}= 8\,\textrm{TeV}$, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $20\,\textrm{fb}^{-1}$. The measured branching fractions for these decays are $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S) = (3.2 \pm 0.5 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.3)\times 10^{-4}$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S) = (1.9 \pm 0.4 \pm 0.2 \pm 0.2)\times 10^{-4}$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second combines systematic errors.

Constructing the submodule lattice for an arbitrary module over a commutative ring is notoriously difficult, a challenge that is particularly acute for modules with positive characteristic zero. This paper introduces a novel algorithm designed to build the submodule lattice for a specific class of modules: those with a multiplicity-free structure over a polynomial ring in one variable with coefficients in a field of characteristic zero. The algorithm operates by first decomposing the module into its primary components, which are then processed individually. For each primary component, the algorithm applies a specialized construction method. The resulting lattice is expressed as a join-semilattice, where the join operation is defined by a canonical form. The paper concludes with a detailed examination of the algorithm's computational complexity.

A set of words over an alphabet $\Sigma$ is $p/q$-recognisable if the language formed by the residues modulo $p/q$ of the values of a specific morphism from $\Sigma^*$ to $\mathbb{Z}$, defined by $\sigma(n_0 + \sum_{i=1}^k n_i \sigma^i) = \sum_{i=1}^k n_i \sigma^i + n_0$, constitutes a regular language. This paper establishes a regularity criterion for the image of a rational relation under such a morphism, thereby demonstrating that the image of a rational relation is $p/q$-recognisable only when finite. Additionally, the authors prove that the union and intersection of $p/q$-recognisable sets are always $P/Q$-recognisable for some $P/Q$, and they provide a regularity condition for the image of a regular language under a rational relation to be $p/q$-recognisable.

The peeling of adhesive tape from a rigid surface is a nonlinear process driven by the complex interplay between the tape's elastic properties and the adhesive's characteristics. This study employs acoustic emission (AE) techniques to investigate the stick-slip dynamics inherent in this phenomenon. We demonstrate that the resulting stick-slip motion exhibits clear signatures of self-organized criticality, indicating the presence of deterministic, ordered behavior within the system's apparent chaotic noise. Specifically, we reveal that the noise adheres to a universal power-law distribution and satisfies the Bouchaud trap model. These findings collectively suggest that the system operates under critical conditions, governed by deterministic dynamics rather than purely stochastic ones.

In 1923, in his seminal paper on metric spaces, K. Menger introduced spaces defined by a single metric function, which he termed "angle spaces." He proposed two unresolved problems regarding these spaces, both of which were addressed by the current authors. The first problem was solved by the first author in 1964, and the second by the second author in 1964.

Neural network architectures for point clouds have recently gained traction, yet their training predominantly relies on large-scale datasets like ShapeNet and ModelNet40/CAIR. These datasets are often smoothed to mitigate noise and enhance generalization, a technique known as smoothing. However, smoothing can inadvertently degrade performance on specific tasks, such as classification, where it may obscure distinctive characteristics introduced by data transformations. To address this, we introduce Transformation-Specific Smoothing (TPC), a method designed to retain essential transformation features while still improving generalization. Our approach combines a transformation-aware smoothing mechanism with a specialized unlearning module that recovers lost transformation details. Experiments demonstrate that TPc surpasses conventional smoothing strategies across various classification benchmarks and exhibits notable success when applied to real-world scenarios involving physical deformations.

Formal verification offers a rigorous approach to ensuring program correctness, yet it often encounters scalability hurdles and remains inaccessible to many practitioners. Conversely, testing provides a practical alternative, but its effectiveness relies heavily on the selection of test cases, which is currently guided by ad-hoc strategies. This paper introduces a geometric framework designed to enhance testing efficacy. By modeling programs as geometric structures, the theory identifies specific configurations that guarantee the detection of all bugs within a program. Furthermore, it establishes a lower bound for the geometric complexity required to uncover a particular bug. The authors validate this theory through a case study of a sorting algorithm, demonstrating that the geometric approach successfully identifies bugs that traditional testing methods overlook.

We present an explicit formula for the Serre weight conjecture for unramified $\mathrm{GL}_2$ over a totally real field, utilizing Kummer theory. This approach offers a more direct alternative to the method developed by Calegari and Emerton, which relies on the local Langlands correspondence.

Fiber-reinforced composites containing conductive fillers exhibit changes in electrical conductivity when subjected to mechanical strain, a property that enables self-sensing capabilities for structural health monitoring. This study investigates damage detection and characterization in unidirectional glass fiber-reinforced vinyl ester composites with 0.5% short carbon fiber fillings. By combining electrical impedance tomography (EIT) with a genetic algorithm (GA), the research achieves high-precision damage mapping. The EIT technique provides surface conductivity images, while the GA reconstructs the internal conductivity distribution from these 2D visualizations. Experimental results demonstrate that the integrated EIT/GA framework successfully identifies and quantifies damage caused by 0.5 mm and 1.0 mm notches. Specifically, the system accurately recovers the conductivity variations within the notch region, revealing a conductivity increase of approximately 100% for the 0.5 mm notch and 200% for the 1.0 mm notch. These findings confirm the viability of the proposed method for detecting and characterizing damage in self-sensing composite materials.

This paper examines the geometric approach to describing a Euclidean space, contrasting it with the tensor approach. We demonstrate that geometric descriptions are more concise and intuitively clear, particularly when dealing with the transformation of a basis. Additionally, we show that geometric descriptions offer a more intuitive understanding of the metric tensor.

We examine splittings of right-angled Artin groups (RAAGs) that are compatible with the standard generators. Specifically, we analyze how these splittings relate to the defining graph of the RAAG and demonstrate that they correspond to edge subdivisions within the graph.

Iterative techniques for matrix inversion are highly attractive for large-scale matrices because they require significantly less memory than direct methods and can be efficiently parallelized on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). This paper introduces a novel iteration method designed to enhance the convergence speed of these iterative approaches. Building upon the Neumann series, the proposed technique employs a specific transformation to generate a new iteration function, which is then utilized within a fixed-point iteration framework. The authors demonstrate that this new method achieves a higher order of convergence compared to standard iterations. Furthermore, the study provides a theoretical analysis of the relationship between the iteration's order and the transformation matrix, offering guidance for selecting optimal transformation matrices. To validate the approach, the paper presents both theoretical findings and empirical results, including a demonstration of the method's application to the inversion of massive matrices.

Contextual linear bandits (CLBs) are a prominent class of contextual bandits that have been extensively studied in distributed environments. In these setups, multiple agents operate across distinct nodes, each possessing unique local data and collaborating to learn an optimal policy. A primary hurdle in this domain is the communication overhead required to exchange data or model parameters between nodes. This paper introduces a novel distributed algorithm designed for CLBs that operates without the need to share context vectors between nodes. The proposed method combines local stochastic gradient descent (SGD) steps with periodic averaging of the learned contextual linear weight parameters. We establish theoretical bounds for both the regret and the communication costs associated with this approach. Specifically, our regret bound mirrors that of centralized CLBs up to logarithmic factors, while the communication overhead is shown to be nearly optimal. Additionally, we provide a matching lower bound for the communication complexity, demonstrating the optimality of our proposed solution.

We examine the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, focusing on how dust evolution influences it. By utilizing a two-fluid approach that incorporates dust, we find that the VSI remains active in the disk's midplane even after dust growth and radial drift have caused the atmosphere to become stable. In these scenarios, dust-driven convection emerges as a viable mechanism for transporting angular momentum outward, thereby facilitating disk evolution.

We establish a Liouville theorem for complete Ricci shrinkers that possess constant scalar curvature and are either Liouville or Liouville with respect to bounded harmonic functions. As a consequence, we demonstrate that compact Liouville or Liouville with respect to bounded harmonic function Ricci shrinkers must be shrinking gradient Ricci solitons.

Backdoor attacks represent a significant threat to deep learning systems, where adversaries inject malicious behaviors into models during training by introducing specific triggers associated with target labels. While prior research has extensively examined static backdoors—where the trigger remains constant across all poisoned samples—this study investigates dynamic backdoors, which employ varying triggers to achieve the same objective. We demonstrate that global average pooling (GAP), a prevalent layer in convolutional neural networks (CNNs), inadvertently facilitates these dynamic backdoors. Our findings reveal that dynamic backdoors do not merely alter a model's output for triggered inputs; they also cause the model to misclassify clean, untriggered data as the target class. To address this vulnerability, we propose a novel defense mechanism designed to eliminate dynamic backdoors. Evaluations on three distinct datasets indicate that our approach successfully removes these attacks while preserving the accuracy of legitimate classifications.

The rapid rise of Internet-of-Things (IoT) and mobile devices has generated vast amounts of data, yet privacy concerns and communication constraints hinder centralized processing. Federated learning (FL) offers a promising solution by enabling collaborative model training directly on local devices without exchanging raw data. However, existing FL methods often falter when confronted with the reality of heterogeneous data distributions across non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) sources. To address these challenges, we introduce Walk for Learning (W4L), a novel random walk framework designed to adapt to data heterogeneity. In this approach, a server initiates a random walk by selecting a starting node; the walk then proceeds by moving to a neighboring node chosen with probability proportional to that node's data volume. Upon visiting a new node, the server retrieves the local model trained at that site and integrates it into the global model via an averaging process. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that W4L achieves convergence rates comparable to those of standard FL methods, while requiring significantly less communication overhead. Furthermore, extensive experiments confirm that W4L attains superior performance relative to current state-of-the-art approaches.

Although deep learning has achieved remarkable success in medical image segmentation using only labeled data, the scarcity of annotated images in clinical settings often hinders the deployment of these advanced models. To overcome this, semi-supervised approaches have been developed to leverage abundant unlabeled images. However, these methods frequently suffer from overfitting and fail to generalize well. This paper introduces ConsReg, a novel regularization technique designed to enhance the consistency of segmentation predictions across different augmented versions of unlabeled images. ConsReg operates by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the predicted segmentations from an unlabeled image and the average prediction derived from its augmented counterparts. Our experiments demonstrate that ConsReg consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across various datasets. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that the proposed regularization significantly reduces overfitting and improves generalization capabilities.

Although single-particle entanglement is often dismissed as merely a mathematical artifact with no physical significance, we demonstrate here that it actually enables genuinely nonlocal phenomena. Specifically, we show that single-particle entanglement can produce steering effects, which are strictly stronger than Bell nonlocality. These results indicate that single-particle entanglement is not just a formal quirk but a resource capable of generating authentic nonlocal behavior.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) holds significant promise for enhancing traffic safety, optimizing traffic flow, and improving overall road infrastructure. However, the distributed and vast nature of IoVs data presents challenges regarding privacy and security, which are critical for sensitive user information. Simultaneously, the computational and storage limitations of IoVs devices hinder the processing of massive datasets. To overcome these hurdles, Federated Learning (FL) offers a viable solution by enabling collaborative model training across distributed data sources without requiring raw data centralization. Furthermore, Blockchain technology provides robust security, privacy, and trust mechanisms essential for IoVs applications. This paper presents a comprehensive survey examining Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning (BEFL) frameworks designed for IoVs. The analysis explores various BEFL architectures, key challenges, and potential solutions. Additionally, it investigates the roles of Blockchain and FL within IoVs, along with the specific benefits and obstacles associated with BEFL implementations. Finally, the study outlines future research trajectories for BEFL within IoVs.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks have become a standard for processing sequential data, yet their substantial computational and memory demands often hinder efficient deployment on hardware with strict resource constraints. This paper introduces an energy-efficient LSTM architecture specifically designed for video recognition tasks, leveraging hierarchical Tucker (HT) tensor decomposition to compress the network's weight matrices. The proposed approach jointly optimizes the LSTM algorithm and the target hardware, resulting in a model that retains high recognition accuracy while significantly reducing both memory footprint and energy usage. Experimental results demonstrate that the HT-LSTM achieves a 2.5× speedup and a 2.1× reduction in energy consumption compared to conventional LSTMs when evaluated on the TIMIT speech dataset and the UCF-101 video dataset.

We demonstrate that the iterates of the composed polynomial $F \circ G$ are monic with integer coefficients and share the same leading coefficient as the iterates of $F$ and $G$. Furthermore, we establish that the iterates of $F \circ G$ are specialized to prime numbers precisely when the iterates of $F$ and $G$ are simultaneously specialized to prime numbers. These results are extended to the case where $F$ and $G$ are monic polynomials defined over the ring of integers in a number field.

We examine the mass-supercritical focusing nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation in the domain outside a smooth, strictly convex obstacle. Building upon recent findings regarding global well-posedness and the dynamics of solutions exceeding the ground state mass, we establish the occurrence of finite-time blow-up for data with positive energy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such solutions exhibit asymptotic behavior akin to a traveling soliton as time approaches the singularity.

We establish a characteristic-zero to positive-characteristic lifting theorem for varieties defined by local uniform semi-parametric equations. This result serves as a local variant of the local uniform reduction principle originally developed by Ayoub.

Bayesian hypothesis testing offers a compelling alternative to frequentist methods, particularly for small datasets, yet its adoption has been hindered by the computational intensity of standard approaches. Although recent advances have made Bayesian analysis more accessible, calculating Bayes factors (BFs) for complex, realistic models often remains difficult. This paper introduces a practical workflow designed to compute BFs reliably for intricate models, combining a novel, adaptable prior predictive checking method with a robust MCMC-based calculation strategy. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through an analysis of the famous "Lady Tasting Tea" dataset, showing how the workflow successfully quantifies the strength of evidence for a complex hierarchical model compared to simpler alternatives.

Discourse markers (DMs) are crucial for conveying the logical relationships between sentences, yet their semantic nuances are notoriously difficult to capture using standard semantic similarity measures. This study introduces DiscSense, a novel framework designed to analyze the semantics of English DMs. The approach combines a knowledge graph with a neural network to generate a semantic representation for each marker. Evaluated against human-constructed similarity judgments across various tasks, DiscSense demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the model uncovers specific semantic characteristics of English DMs, revealing that their meanings are often context-dependent and exhibit distinct patterns regarding the polarity of the relations they signal.

We examine the Jordanian twist introduced by D'Antoni and Longo, which was originally defined for the universal enveloping algebra of a specific three-dimensional solvable Lie algebra. By extending the Jordanian twist to the universal enveloping algebra of a nine-dimensional solvable Lie algebra, we examine the resulting braided structure. We demonstrate that this extended twist generates a braiding that is not universal, and we provide a concrete example of a representation where the associated braiding operator fails to be unique.

Regular expressions are fundamental for text processing and feature matching in numerous applications. Although standard regex operators like union, concatenation, and Kleene star are well-established, they lack support for inequality comparisons. This paper introduces extended regular expressions, which incorporate these inequalities, and presents a method to solve the resulting inequations symbolically. The approach transforms the problem into solving a system of regular inequations, which are then converted into a set of regular equations solved via a novel algorithm. This algorithm combines a decision procedure for regular languages with a constraint solver for rational languages. The method is implemented in the Coq proof assistant, where the associated decision procedures and the solution algorithm are formally verified. Additionally, the implementation includes a decision procedure for regular inequations. Experimental results indicate that the tool successfully solves complex regex inequations, surpassing the capabilities of existing approaches.

Building upon the work of P. Li, we examine OPE blocks composed of spinning primary operators within AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$. We demonstrate that these blocks can be expressed as a sum of AdS$_3$ single-trace fields, where the AdS$_3$ mass and spin serve as the summation indices. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between this decomposition and the AdS$_3$ Kato–Odake (KO) equation.

We propose a concept for wide-field X-ray monitors utilizing lobster-eye optics that employs multiplexing to enhance detection sensitivity. This approach involves combining the focal images from numerous lobster-eye modules onto a single detector, thereby increasing the effective field of view and reducing the overall system cost. We present a detailed analysis of the imaging characteristics for this multiplexed configuration and evaluate the sensitivity gains achievable through this method.

This study examines the influence of the cosmic velocity field on the dark matter halo mass function (HM) across the linear and mildly non-linear regimes. Utilizing $N$-body simulations, we find that the velocity field induces a non-monotonic modification to the HM, causing it to shift toward lower masses at both the onset of non-linearity and within the highly non-linear regime. We attribute this behavior to the velocity field's tendency to concentrate dark matter in high-density regions, thereby reducing the effective collapse threshold. To investigate this phenomenon, we apply a deep learning approach to analyze the non-linear relationship between the HM and velocity dispersion. Our results indicate that velocity dispersion acts as a proxy for the velocity field's impact on the HM, with the effect becoming increasingly pronounced as non-linearity grows.

We report the detection of local magnetic field variations with a sensitivity of 0.02 nT/√Hz at 1 Hz, achieved by integrating an atomic interferometer with a superconducting Meissner sensor. This setup measures the displacement of a superconducting plate caused by the magnetic field, which in turn alters the phase of an atomic interferometer. We demonstrate that the system's sensitivity is primarily constrained by technical noise from the magnetic field measurement rather than fundamental quantum limits. Consequently, the sensitivity can be enhanced by improving the precision of the magnetic field detection.

We present a relativistic first-principles investigation of the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states generated by magnetic adatoms and adatomic dimers on a superconducting surface. Specifically, we examine an Mn adatom and Mn dimers situated on the Nb(110) surface. Our analysis reveals that the local magnetic moments of the Mn configurations are reduced by the proximity effect, with the magnitude of this reduction varying according to the specific atomic arrangement. Furthermore, we observe a clear correlation between the local density of states (LDOS) and the spin-resolved LDOS (SLDOS), a relationship that enables the identification of the y-axis crossing in the differential conductance ($dI/dV$) spectroscopy data. Finally, we demonstrate that the energy of the YSR states can be accurately predicted by the Kondo temperature ($T_K$) derived from the local magnetic moments.

Skin cancer detection is a critical task in computer vision, yet it faces significant challenges due to the scarcity of high-quality training data and the presence of outlier samples. This paper introduces a novel deep learning architecture designed to address these issues, combining a ResNet-50 backbone with a multi-scale attention mechanism to enhance feature extraction. The proposed model employs a two-stage training strategy: first, it is pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset, and subsequently, it undergoes fine-tuning on the specific skin lesion dataset. To ensure robustness against outliers, the method incorporates an outlier detection module based on entropy, which identifies anomalous samples within the training set. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves a 98.7% accuracy rate on the ISIC 2018 dataset, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the system exhibits strong generalization capabilities, successfully detecting outliers in unseen datasets.

At high-energy muon collisions, the process of electroweak boson radiation becomes prominent, enabling the treatment of W and Z bosons as effective constituents within the muon. This paper examines the validity of the Effective W Approximation (EWA) and its extension, the Effective $W$ Approximation (E$\W$A), specifically for the production of $t\bar{t}$ pairs and $WZ$ boson final states. Our analysis indicates that while the EWA offers a reliable estimate for leading-order (LO) cross sections at the 20\% level for $\sqrt{s} = 10\,\text{TeV}$ muon collisions, it tends to overestimate results when non-polarized muons are considered. Furthermore, we find that incorporating subleading corrections significantly enhances the precision of the EWA.

This paper demonstrates that the diagonal lemma holds true for the arithmetized version of Carnap's 1934 semantics for first-order logic, a system which incorporates Godel's incompleteness theorems, Tarski's undefinability of truth, and Rosser's strengthening of Godel's second theorem. We provide a reconstruction of the lemma's proof within this framework, showing how it can be used to derive Godel's two theorems, Tarski's result, and Rosser's theorem. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the diagonal lemma and Godel's $\beta$-function, which serves as a specific instance of the lemma.

Invariant sets, including invariant manifolds, are fundamental to the study of dynamical systems. This paper examines invariant sets for fractional order systems defined by the Caputo fractional derivative. We establish that the fractional order system $\dot{x} = f(t,x)$, where $f$ is continuous and satisfies a Lipschitz condition with respect to $x$, admits an invariant set $M$ only if $M$ is a single point. Consequently, the system possesses no invariant manifolds of dimension greater than zero. These findings are extended to fractional order systems with variable coefficients and those involving fractional order terms.

This study examines the inverse problem involving a structural acoustic interaction, where the goal is to determine the time-varying boundary traction applied to a semi-infinite elastic half-space. This traction is deduced from the measurement of acoustic pressure within the fluid domain. The analysis establishes the well-posedness of the problem and derives a unique solution for the traction. Furthermore, a constructive algorithm for recovering this traction is proposed, relying on a Carleman estimate.

We examine the scoto-seesaw model, extending the simplest variant by incorporating an additional right-handed neutrino and a pair of inert Higgs doublets. This extension enables the simultaneous explanation of neutrino masses, dark matter, and the origin of electroweak symmetry breaking via vacuum stability. We analyze the parameter space to determine the conditions under which the model remains viable, focusing on the stability of the vacuum, the mechanism of neutrino mass generation, and the phenomenology of dark matter. Our findings indicate that the model remains consistent with current experimental constraints across a wide range of parameters, with the dark matter candidate being a neutral scalar that decays exclusively into neutrinos.
